title: What is the Strategy pattern, where does it appear in the Java standard library, and how does it enforce the Open/Closed Principle (payment-strategy example)?
shortTitle: What is the Strategy pattern and how does it enforce the Open/Closed Principle
keyPoints: Strategy defines a family of interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, chosen at runtime.
Three parts: strategy interface, concrete strategies, and a context that holds and delegates to a strategy.
Enforces OCP: adding a new algorithm is a new class, never an edit to existing code.
Java standard library examples: Comparator, RejectedExecutionHandler, Collector.
In modern Java, a single-method strategy is a functional interface, so a lambda replaces a named class.
In Spring, injecting a Map of bean name to strategy gives runtime selection with zero factory code.

s1_definition.oneliner: Strategy makes algorithms interchangeable behind one interface, chosen at runtime, so adding a new algorithm is a new class, never an edit to old code.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Strategy pattern** – defines a family of interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface and lets the algorithm be selected at runtime.
- **Context** – holds a reference to the strategy interface and delegates to whichever concrete strategy it was given, without knowing which one.
- **Open/Closed** – adding a new algorithm means adding a new strategy class rather than editing existing code.
- **Functional fit** – in Java, a single-method strategy interface is a `@FunctionalInterface`, so a lambda or method reference can replace a named class.
s1_definition.analogy: When Rajesh pays at the National Bank of India, he can choose UPI, card, or net banking. The payment counter does not care which he picks; it just runs whatever payment method he hands it. Each payment method is a self-contained strategy, and adding a new one like a wallet means opening a new method lane without touching the existing lanes. The counter stays the same; only the chosen method changes.

```text
  ──────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │    PaymentContext     │
  │ ─────────────────     │
  │ - strategy: Strategy  │
  │ + checkout(amount)    │──── delegates ────▶ strategy.pay(amount)
  └──────────────────────┘
           │
           │ holds reference to
           ▼
  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │  PaymentStrategy     │ ◄── interface
  │  + pay(amount)       │
  └──────────┬───────────┘
             │
     ┌───────┼────────┬──────────┐
     ▼       ▼        ▼          ▼
  ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐
  │ UPI  │ │ Card │ │ Net  │ │Wallet│
  │      │ │      │ │ Bank │ │ (new)│
  └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘

  Adding Wallet = new class only
  Context + existing strategies: UNTOUCHED
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Strategy pattern defines a family of interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface and lets Rajesh choose the algorithm at runtime. It has three parts: a strategy interface that declares the algorithm, concrete strategies that implement it differently, and a context that holds a strategy and delegates to it without knowing which concrete one it has. The whole point is that the context depends only on the interface, so algorithms swap freely.

It appears all over the Java standard library. The clearest example is `Comparator`, where Rajesh plugs a comparison algorithm into a fixed sort. The thread pool's `RejectedExecutionHandler` is a strategy for what to do when the queue is full, the `Collector` in the Streams API is a strategy, and even a `Runnable` handed to a thread is a pluggable unit of behaviour.

Strategy enforces the Open/Closed Principle directly. At the National Bank of India, Pankaj once broke the card payment branch while adding net banking to a growing switch statement, which caused failed card payments in production. With Strategy, each payment method is its own class implementing `PaymentStrategy`, the checkout context just looks it up and delegates, and adding a wallet method is a new class registered in a map with zero edits to the context or the existing strategies.

In modern Java, a Strategy is often just a lambda because a single-method interface is a functional interface, so Rajesh can write an interest strategy as a one-line lambda. In Spring, injecting a `Map<String, PaymentStrategy>` gives runtime selection for free, so adding a payment method is literally adding a new bean.

Remember one sentence: Strategy makes algorithms interchangeable behind one interface, enforcing OCP because adding a new algorithm is a new class, never an edit.
